title: Types and values
Types and values
Reading and writing
text:
read_* functions return a DataFrame. scan_* functions return a LazyFrame, so filters and column selections are pushed into the reader. DataFrame::write*() writes a file; LazyFrame::sink*() streams a query’s result to a file without collecting it in memory.
read_database($query, $pdo) reads a query’s result from any PDO connection. params binds placeholders through prepare() and execute(). schemaOverrides casts columns afterwards, which helps with drivers that return numbers or dates as strings: ['d' => 'Date'] parses ISO date text.
$df->writeDatabase('table', $pdo) inserts the rows in batches inside a transaction and returns the row count. ifTableExists is fail (the default), append, or replace. A new table gets portable column types: BIGINT, DOUBLE PRECISION, TEXT, BOOLEAN, DATE, and TIMESTAMP (DATETIME(6) on MySQL). List and struct values are stored as JSON text. It is tested against SQLite, PostgreSQL 17, and MySQL 8.4.
Parquet, IPC, and JSON support are Cargo features. An extension built without one raises a ComputeError from that format’s functions.

title: DataFrame and LazyFrame
text: DataFrame holds data in memory and runs each operation immediately. LazyFrame records operations and runs them, optimized, on collect(). Both have the same verbs; a DataFrame builds each verb on a lazy query and collects it, as py-polars does.

text:
Joins
join() takes on, or leftOn and rightOn, and how: inner, left, right, full, semi, anti, or cross. suffix names clashing right-hand columns, coalesce merges key columns, nullsEqual lets null keys match, and maintainOrder (none, left, right, left_right, right_left) fixes the row order.
$sales = read_csv('sales.csv')->select('id', 'store', 'units')->head(6);
$stores = read_csv('stores.csv')->filter(col('store')->ne('S2'));

echo $sales->join($stores, on: 'store', how: 'left', maintainOrder: 'left'), "\n";
echo $sales->join($stores, on: 'store', how: 'anti'), "\n";
echo $stores->rename(['store' => 'shop'])->join($sales, leftOn: 'shop', rightOn: 'store', how: 'inner')->height(), " matched rows\n";

text:
Time series
groupByDynamic() groups rows into fixed time windows, and rolling() gives each row a window that ends at it. joinAsof() matches each row to the nearest earlier (or later, or nearest) row of another frame, optionally within by groups and a tolerance. Durations are py-polars strings such as '1d', '2h30m', '1w', and '1mo'. Expressions add the rolling*By() family and ewmMean(). The functions date_range() and datetime_range() build calendars.
$daily = read_csv('sales.csv', tryParseDates: true)
    ->groupBy('date')->agg(col('units')->sum())
    ->sort('date');

// Weeks starting on Monday.
echo $daily->groupByDynamic('date', every: '1w')->agg(col('units')->sum()->alias('week_units'))->head(3), "\n";

// The seven days ending at each row.
echo $daily->withColumns(col('units')->rollingSumBy('date', '7d')->alias('last_7d'))->head(4), "\n";

// The list price in force on each day.
$prices = (new DataFrame(['from' => [new DateTimeImmutable('2024-01-01'), new DateTimeImmutable('2024-01-05')], 'list_price' => [5.0, 5.5]]))
    ->cast(['from' => 'Date']);
echo $daily->head(4)->joinAsof($prices, leftOn: 'date', rightOn: 'from');

title: Performance
text:
Where the time goes
Polars runs the verbs themselves 10 to 100 times faster than the in-memory frame. Returning rows to PHP is the cost that remains. Collecting 1M rows into PHP takes about 0.2 s for plain columns, plus about 0.5 s per datetime column, because each DateTimeImmutable is a PHP object.
PolarsTable is the faster backend when a pipeline reduces the data (summaries, filters, joins followed by summaries) or chains several verbs before collecting. Reading files with Phpolars\read_csv() or read_parquet() and wrapping the result with PolarsTable::fromPolars() also avoids parsing the file in PHP.
A verb given a PHP closure converts the table to a phibble DataFrame and back, about 1 s per million rows with a datetime column. On large data, use expressions, or use phibble’s in-memory DataFrame for closure-heavy pipelines.

title: Deployment
text:
Prebuilt binaries
The packaging workflow builds the extension inside the official php:8.3-fpm-bookworm, php:8.4-fpm-bookworm, and php:8.5-fpm-bookworm images, installs it with PIE, runs the release checks, and sends real requests through PHP-FPM. It then packages each tested php_polars.so for x86_64 and arm64 in a zip named as PIE expects, such as php_php_polars-v0.2.0_php8.4-x86_64-linux-glibc-nts.zip, with:

manifest.json: PHP version and API number, architecture, glibc, the Rust version, the Cargo.lock hash, and the extension’s SHA-256.
THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.txt: the licenses of every Rust dependency compiled into the binary.
INSTALL.txt: copy the file to php-config --extension-dir, add extension=php_polars.so, and set php_polars.max_threads.

Release builds attach the six archives to the GitHub release. After publishing, the release workflow installs each one into a clean PHP image by hand and again with pie install, which must pick the prebuilt archive without a Rust toolchain. The binaries are built on Debian Bookworm, need glibc 2.34 or later (Debian 12, Ubuntu 22.04, RHEL 9, or newer), and do not run on Alpine (musl). Other platforms build from source with PIE.

title: Deployment
text:
Threads under PHP-FPM
Polars runs queries on a thread pool. FPM workers are separate processes, so each worker that uses phpolars starts its own pool. The INI setting caps the pool per process:
; php.ini
extension=php_polars.so
php_polars.max_threads = 2
The setting defaults to 2 and is PHP_INI_SYSTEM, because the pool starts once per process and cannot be resized. An explicit POLARS_MAX_THREADS environment variable takes precedence. Phpolars\thread_pool_size() reports the size in effect. Size it so that pm.max_children × max_threads fits the machine’s cores.
PHP closures never run on Polars threads. Every phpolars operation is built from expressions that Polars evaluates natively.

title: Deployment
text:
Memory
Polars allocates with its own allocator, outside PHP’s memory manager, so its memory does not count against memory_limit. Reading a 1M-row CSV raises a process’s resident memory to about 83 MB while memory_get_peak_usage() reports 2 MB. Size FPM pools by process memory, and limit request data with the application’s own checks.

title: Coming from py-polars
Coming from py-polars
text:
Values
Results come back as PHP values: int, float, bool, string, null, DateTimeImmutable for dates and datetimes, lists for List columns, and associative arrays for Struct columns. See Types and values.

title: Coming from py-polars
text:
Names PHP reserves
PHP keywords cannot be function names, so a few functions take a trailing underscore, as struct_() does: var_(), and the selectors cs\list_(), cs\array_(), cs\empty_(), and cs\enum_(). Methods keep their py names, because PHP allows keywords there: $expr->struct(), $expr->list().

title: Coming from py-polars
text:
Python callables
py-polars methods that run a Python function per value or per batch, such as map_elements, map_batches, fold, and map_groups, have no phpolars equivalent. Polars runs expressions on its own threads, and PHP code cannot run there. Use expressions instead. DataFrame::mapRows() is the exception: it runs on the PHP thread, after collecting, and calls a PHP callable per row.

title: Coming from py-polars
text:
Small differences

Series::count() keeps py’s meaning (non-null values). Series does not implement Countable; use len().
__toString() gives Polars’ table layout, so echo $df prints like print(df).
DataFrame::toColumns() is a phpolars addition: toDict(asSeries: false).
Strings in arithmetic are literals in phpolars, as they are in comparisons. py treats a string as a column name in some operators (col("a") - "b") but not others (col("a") + "b"); use col('b') for a column.
Series and DataFrame methods never change the object in place. py’s in-place methods (scatter, set, extend, insert_column, replace_column) return a new object.
read_database() takes a PDO connection.

title: phpolars
text: phpolars brings Polars to PHP as a native extension written in Rust. It follows the py-polars API: the same classes, methods, and semantics, with camelCase method names and snake_case functions. A test suite compares 314 cases against py-polars 1.43.2, and all of them match.

title: phpolars
text:
What it includes

DataFrame and LazyFrame with py-polars’ verbs: select, withColumns, filter, sort, groupBy/agg, join, unique, pivot, unpivot, explode, describe, and more.
Expressions with arithmetic, three-valued logic, aggregations, window functions (over), when/then/otherwise, and the str, dt, list, struct, and name namespaces.
Series, with the same expression methods.
CSV, Parquet, JSON, NDJSON, and Arrow IPC reading and writing, with lazy scans and streaming sinks.
A thread-pool cap for PHP-FPM (php_polars.max_threads).
A backend for phibble, Phibble\Polars\PolarsTable, that runs phplyr pipelines in Polars. It ships with phibble ^0.2; see phibble’s Backends page.

title: phpolars
text:
The family
phpolars is one of a set of PHP 8.3+ packages for data work. phibble is a pure-PHP data frame and the shared table contract. phplyr adds dplyr verbs on top of it. phit fits regression and mixed models. phpolars is the optional fast backend: install it when the data is large or the pipeline is heavy, and keep using phplyr’s verbs.

title: phibble and phplyr
text:
phibble defines a table contract with several backends: its in-memory DataFrame, SqlTable for PDO databases, and Phibble\Polars\PolarsTable, which runs on a Polars DataFrame when the php_polars extension is loaded. phplyr’s verbs work on any of them, so a phplyr pipeline runs in Polars when it starts from a PolarsTable. The backend ships with phibble ^0.2; install phpolars to enable it. phibble’s Backends page compares the backends.
A phplyr pipeline on a PolarsTable runs in Polars:
$out is a PolarsTable, and $out->collect() returns a Phibble\DataFrame.

title: phibble and phplyr
text:
What runs in Polars
Verbs given column names or phibble expressions (Phibble\Expr, which phplyr’s helpers such as col(), mean(), and n() build) run in Polars with dplyr’s semantics: NA propagates, aggregates default to na_rm = FALSE, grouped mutate() and filter() evaluate aggregates and windows per group, groups follow sorted key order, and joins follow dplyr 1.2, including join_by() inequality and rolling joins. Pivots, stringr and lubridate functions, and phibble’s reference fixtures all run natively.
PHP closures cannot run on Polars threads. A verb given a closure converts the table to a phibble DataFrame, runs there, and converts the result back; PolarsTable::$fallbacks counts these conversions. See Performance for their cost.
PolarsTable::fromTable() throws when a list column would not round-trip exactly, for example when named arrays with different keys would become structs.

title: phibble and phplyr
text:
Moving data directly
Without the backend, DataFrame::fromPhibble($table) reads any phibble table through toColumns(), and $df->toPhibble() returns a Phibble\DataFrame, which needs phibble v0.2 or later.

title: Expressions
text:
An Expr describes a computation on columns. Expressions are built with col(), lit(), when(), and the other functions below, and are evaluated by frame verbs such as select(), withColumns(), filter(), and agg(). They never hold PHP closures, so Polars runs them on its own threads.
Operands of comparison and arithmetic methods may be an Expr or a PHP value. PHP strings there are string literals.

title: Expressions

echo $sales->select(
    'date',
    'product',
    'units',
    col('units')->sum()->over('product')->alias('product_total'),
    col('units')->cumSum()->over('product', orderBy: 'date')->alias('running'),
    col('units')->shift()->over('product', orderBy: 'date')->alias('previous'),
    col('units')->rank('dense', descending: true)->alias('rank'),
);
